t.E270.agn: Humans have consumed soured milk and fermented products containing lactic acid for centuries. In 1973 JECFA set the ADI for lactic acid and its salts as 'not limited'; in 2001 it saw no safety concern at current intake levels as a flavouring substance. JECFA has reported that infants in their first three months have difficulty metabolising DL- and D(-)-lactic acid and has recommended that these forms not be used in infant foods.
t.E270.body: L(+)-lactate is a normal intermediate of mammalian metabolism and is largely converted to glycogen in the liver; the D(-) form is used more slowly.
t.E270.eff.0.w: Everyone except infants in their first three months
t.E270.eff.1.t: Infants in their first three months have difficulty metabolising DL- and D(-)-lactic acid; JECFA recommended that these forms not be used in infant foods
t.E270.eff.1.w: Infants in their first three months
t.E270.found.0: May be used in many foods in the EU at quantum satis (as much as needed)
t.E270.found.1: Infant formulae and complementary foods for infants (in the EU only under limited conditions, such as pH adjustment)
t.E270.prod: Produced by lactic fermentation of sugars or by chemical synthesis.
t.E270.pw.0: JECFA has recommended that D(-)- and DL-lactic acid not be used in infant foods; in the EU only the L(+) form is permitted in infant formulae and complementary foods for infants.
t.E270.regx.0: ADI 'not limited'; the D(-) and DL forms should not be used in infant foods.
t.E270.regx.1: Group I additive; generally authorised at quantum satis (as much as needed).
t.E270.regx.2: Only the L(+) form is permitted in infant formulae and complementary foods for infants.
t.E270.summary: The acid formed by fermentation that gives yoghurt and pickles their sourness. Today it is usually produced by fermenting sugar or starch; it is used as an acidity regulator.
t.E270.what: It is an acidity regulator that adds sourness to food and adjusts pH.
